The circle of sky your binoculars show at once. Its width in degrees is printed on most binoculars.
A pulsing supergiant that brightens and fades on a strict rhythm. The slower the rhythm, the more light it really gives off.
The other star in a pair, usually the fainter one.
One of 88 official regions of the sky, each named after the old star figure inside it, such as Orion or Cygnus.
A cold cloud of dust thick enough to block the stars behind it, seen as a dark patch.
Two stars that look close together. Some orbit each other; others only line up by chance.
When a giant's churning layers carry freshly made elements, such as carbon, up from its core to its surface.
Two stars whose orbit we see edge-on, so they take turns passing in front of each other and the light dips.
Atoms crushed together in a star's core into heavier ones, releasing the energy that makes the star shine.
The flat, spinning pancake of stars, gas and dust where the Sun and most young stars of our galaxy live.
The huge, thin sphere of old stars and globular clusters surrounding a galaxy's flat disk.
The second-lightest element. Stars make it by fusing hydrogen, and heavier stars later fuse it into carbon and oxygen.
The lightest and most common element, the main fuel stars burn for most of their lives.
The rarest, most luminous kind of supergiant: so bloated and unstable it sheds huge amounts of gas.
Light with longer waves than red, invisible to the eye. It passes through dust and shows cool things.
Several telescopes linked to act as one giant one, sharp enough to measure star sizes or split very close pairs.
The distance light travels in one year: about 9.5 trillion km. It measures distance, not time.
The total light a star really gives off, however near or far it is. The Sun's is the usual yardstick.
A huge, unstable blue star that brightens and erupts unpredictably, throwing off shells of gas.
The astronomer's brightness scale. Smaller numbers are brighter; each step of 5 magnitudes is a factor of 100 in brightness.
The long, steady adult stage of a star's life, when it quietly fuses hydrogen in its core, as the Sun does now.
Our home galaxy, and the faint band of light it makes across the sky because we see its disk from inside.
A cloud of gas and dust in space. Some glow, some reflect starlight and some block the light behind them.
A loose family of stars born together from one cloud, usually a few hundred million years old or younger.
Two stars that only look close because they lie in nearly the same direction, at very different distances.
The tiny shift of a nearby star against far ones as Earth circles the Sun. The smaller the shift, the farther the star.
A star still forming: a collapsing ball of gas that is not yet hot enough in its core to fuse hydrogen.
A star that swells and shrinks in a rhythm, getting brighter and fainter as it does.
A small, cool star lighter than the Sun. Such stars burn their fuel so slowly that they outlive every other kind.
An ageing star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to many times its old size, cooling to orange or red.

A cloud of gas and dust where new stars are forming right now.
A heavy star late in life, swollen to enormous size and pouring out thousands of times the Sun's light.
The explosion of a star, briefly outshining a whole galaxy of ordinary stars. Heavy stars end this way.
Light with shorter waves than violet, invisible to the eye. Hot stars pour out lots of it.
A star whose brightness changes, because it pulses, erupts, or is eclipsed by a partner.

journeys.title: Measuring the Depth of Cassiopeia
journeys.drivingQuestion: How can anyone know how far away a star or a galaxy is?
journeys.hook: Every distance in the sky rests on the one below it, and the first on Earth's orbit.
journeys.story: No one has ever measured the distance to another galaxy directly. Tonight's path climbs the ladder that makes it possible, from geometry through families of stars to stars bright enough to be timed in a galaxy of their own.
journeys.payoff: Tonight's ladder left the Milky Way at the Andromeda Galaxy, whose light set out 2.5 million years ago. Below it stood the rungs that make the step possible: geometry for the nearest stars, families of stars for the true power of ordinary ones, and stars of known power bright enough to be picked out in another galaxy. That anyone can date such light at all, from a chain of measurements that begins with Earth's orbit, is one of the quiet wonders of science.

stops.name: Capella

getThere.text: Find Capella by eye, the bright yellow star of Auriga, about 65° up in the north-east. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: Capella opens the ladder with a distance measured as directly as anything in astronomy, by the shift that Earth's own orbit produces.

card.question: How can two giant stars hide inside a single point of light?
card.glance: The golden leader of Auriga, riding high on winter evenings.
card.see: Capella is the brilliant yellowish star high overhead on winter evenings, leading the pentagon of Auriga. Its creamy, slightly golden tint sits halfway between Rigel’s ice and Aldebaran’s orange. Just south of it lies the thin triangle of fainter stars called the Kids.
card.understand: The two stars circle each other every 104 days, so close that only interferometers, which combine several telescopes into one sharp eye, can separate them. Follow the orbit and the same laws that weigh the planets give the masses: about two and a half Suns each. Add each star’s measured size and temperature and something odd appears, because one already burns helium in its core, the fuel of a star’s later years, while its near-twin is only now swelling into a giant.
card.answer: Each giant is about ten times wider than the Sun, yet from 43 light-years their whole orbit shrinks to a speck that only an interferometer can open up.
card.wonder: A difference of a few percent in mass was enough to put two stars born together in different chapters of life.
card.connect: Next door in the Kids, a stranger pair hides one star inside a vast dark disk.

lens.beat: Measured by its yearly shift
lens.question: How far is Capella, and why can that number be trusted?
lens.why: Capella opens the ladder with a distance measured as directly as anything in astronomy, by the shift that Earth's own orbit produces.
lens.look: Capella is the brilliant yellowish star leading Auriga, high overhead on winter evenings. It outshines everything around it, and brightness like that is a hint of closeness, but not yet a measurement.
lens.answer: Hipparcos measured a yearly shift of about 76 thousandths of an arcsecond, which puts Capella about 43 light-years away, and the only assumption behind that number is the size of Earth's orbit. Stars measured this cleanly become reference points for how bright each kind of star truly is, the knowledge the next rungs depend on.
lens.story: Capella offers a rare second route to its distance. Its two stars have been tracked both in angle, by interferometers, and in speed, from the Doppler shift of their light; the speeds give the orbit's true size in kilometers and the interferometers its size in arcseconds, and the ratio of the two is the distance. That orbital parallax agrees with the satellite's yearly shift, two independent rulers meeting on one star.

stops.name: Alpha Persei Cluster

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about three fields of your 6.5° binoculars (20°) to the Alpha Persei Cluster, in Perseus.

stops.whyHere: The Alpha Persei Cluster spreads around Mirfak, a family near enough that Gaia can measure nearly every bright member.
stops.transitionText: Parallax fixed Capella alone; with the Alpha Persei Cluster, the same geometry works on a whole family at once, averaged over hundreds of members.

card.question: What does a star family look like from up close?
card.glance: A loose spray of bright blue-white stars around yellow-white Mirfak, filling the whole field.
card.see: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus, and dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains. It is too big for most telescopes to frame, so binoculars or the eye alone take it in whole.
card.understand: This is an open cluster, a family of stars born together from one cloud, and Gaia picks out its members by their shared motion, like spotting a family walking together through a crowd. Its age comes from a subtle clue: the lightest members slowly destroy the lithium inside them, so the line between stars that still have lithium and those that have lost it works like a clock. Here it reads about 90 million years.
card.answer: Like the Alpha Persei Cluster: at 566 light-years its members spread over several Moon widths, a spray only binoculars can frame. Farther away, the same family would shrink into a small knot.
card.wonder: This family was born while dinosaurs still had tens of millions of years left.
card.connect: The Double Cluster, more than ten times farther away, shows how small a star family looks from across the galaxy.

lens.beat: Hundreds of shifts averaged
lens.question: How does Gaia turn a scattered family around Mirfak into one precise distance?
lens.why: The Alpha Persei Cluster spreads around Mirfak, a family near enough that Gaia can measure nearly every bright member.
lens.look: Center Mirfak and dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains, too big for most telescopes to frame. Mirfak itself fits the family's pattern, a bright member rather than a stranger in front.
lens.answer: Each member's parallax is small and a little uncertain, but averaging nearly a thousand of them shrinks the uncertainty enormously, and the cluster comes out about 566 light-years away. With that distance fixed, the true brightness of every kind of star in it is known, ready to be laid against clusters too far for parallax.
lens.story: The family stands out in Gaia's data as a tight knot in motion: plot every star's drift across the sky and the cluster's members pile into one spot while the field stars scatter. Only after that sorting are the parallaxes combined, and Mirfak, measured on its own, comes out at the family's distance, which is how we know it belongs.

stops.name: Stock 2

getThere.text: Move down and to the left about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (14°), and Stock 2 is there, in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: Stock 2 is a big, loose family beside the Double Cluster, close enough that binoculars show many of the very stars the comparison uses.
stops.transitionText: Lay the stars of Stock 2 against the patterns set by families like the Alpha Persei Cluster, and the gap in brightness becomes a distance, the first rung measured by comparison rather than by geometry.

card.question: Are two clusters side by side in the sky really neighbors?
card.glance: A big, sprawling stick figure of stars in Cassiopeia, arms flexed, about two Moon widths across.
card.see: From the Double Cluster, nudge about two degrees north, and a large loose group fills much of the view; many observers trace a little body with flexed arms, the “Muscleman”. Use the widest field you have, because a telescope is too narrow for it.
card.understand: Gaia measures each member’s parallax and averages them, which pins down a cluster’s distance far better than any single star could. For Stock 2 it gives about 1,200 light-years, and for the Double Cluster over 7,000. The ages differ too: Stock 2 has lost its hottest blue stars, a sign of a few hundred million years, while the Double Cluster’s still blaze.
card.answer: These two are not: Stock 2 is about six times nearer and far older than the glittering pair beside it, proof that clusters touching on the sky can live in completely different parts of the galaxy.
card.wonder: Gaia found about 3,000 members here, a big family hiding in plain sight because it is so spread out.
card.connect: Swing back to the Double Cluster: the nearer family looks bigger and looser, the farther one smaller and denser.

image.caption: Survey photograph of Stock 2, a sprawling cluster two Moon widths across.

lens.beat: Matched against nearer families
lens.question: Before Gaia, how could anyone measure a cluster too far for a clean parallax?
lens.why: Stock 2 is a big, loose family beside the Double Cluster, close enough that binoculars show many of the very stars the comparison uses.
lens.look: Stock 2 fills much of the field two degrees north of the Double Cluster, a loose spray in which some observers trace a little muscleman. Its stars look modest, yet many of them are hotter and more powerful than the Sun, dimmed only by distance.
lens.answer: Plot its steady adult stars by color and brightness, the band astronomers call the main sequence, and slide that band until it lines up with the same band in a cluster of known distance; the amount of sliding is the distance. The method works at any depth where the stars can still be seen, which is how the ladder outruns parallax. Gaia's parallaxes have since checked the slide, and it holds.
lens.story: This family is a hard case for the method because of its sprawl: its members cover more sky than several full Moons, mixed with thousands of unrelated stars in front and behind, which blur any plot of its colors and brightnesses. Before Gaia sorted members by their motions, any fit here had to guess at membership, and Gaia's census is what turned a loose sprinkle into a measured family.

stops.name: Owl Cluster (ET Cluster)

getThere.text: Move down and to the left about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (7°), and the Owl Cluster (ET Cluster) is there, still in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: The Owl Cluster is far enough that its distance rests on its many members together, and that shared distance may also belong to the bright star at its eye.
stops.transitionText: Clusters like Stock 2 do more than measure themselves: together with parallaxes, they fix the true power of the rare stars the next rung relies on, and the Owl Cluster belongs to that rung.

card.question: Does the Owl Cluster’s bright eye really belong to the cluster?
card.glance: Two bright “eyes” at one end of a small, elongated swarm in Cassiopeia, like an owl or the movie alien ET.
card.see: Two degrees south of Ruchbah, find a pair of stars, one much brighter than the other; the bright one is φ Cassiopeiae. A faint, slightly elongated spray trails away from them, and steady binoculars turn it into outstretched wings or arms.
card.understand: The cluster is about 9,100 light-years away and only about 23 million years old. If φ Cassiopeiae belongs to it, it must be a yellow supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life; if it lies in front, it is just an ordinary bright star. Gaia’s parallax for φ Cas matches the cluster’s, but very bright stars are hard for Gaia to measure, and its speed toward us differs somewhat from older values.
card.answer: Probably, since the evidence leans toward membership, which would make the owl’s eye one of the most luminous stars in our galaxy. The case is not closed, and that is part of the fun.
card.wonder: If φ Cas is a member, its light set out about 9,100 years ago, when one of the first towns, Çatalhöyük in Anatolia, was taking shape.
card.connect: M103, a degree from Ruchbah, is a cluster whose stars clearly belong together.

lens.beat: A cluster lends a star its distance
lens.question: How can a single bright star borrow its distance from the cluster around it?
lens.why: The Owl Cluster is far enough that its distance rests on its many members together, and that shared distance may also belong to the bright star at its eye.
lens.look: Two degrees south of Ruchbah, a bright star and a fainter one form the owl's eyes, with a faint elongated spray trailing away as wings. The bright eye is φ Cassiopeiae, the star whose membership is in question.
lens.answer: The cluster's hundreds of members, compared with nearby templates and measured by Gaia, put it about 9,100 light-years away, and a star that truly belongs shares that depth. If φ Cas does, its modest look hides enormous power, and borrowing a distance from a cluster is exactly how rare, powerful stars like the Cepheids had their true output pinned down.
lens.story: Borrowing works only if membership is real, and the test is the usual pair: the star must share the cluster's distance and its motion through space. For φ Cassiopeiae the distance fits while its speed toward us is a little off the cluster's, so astronomers still hedge, and every Cepheid in a cluster had to pass the same scrutiny before it could calibrate anything.

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: Move left about three fields of your 6.5° binoculars (18°), and the Andromeda Galaxy is there, in Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: The Andromeda Galaxy is where the pulsing-star ruler first left the Milky Way, and its history shows how every rung depends on the ones below.
stops.transitionText: From the Owl Cluster the ladder takes its longest step, because the brightest stars of known power can be picked out one by one in the Andromeda Galaxy, far beyond the Milky Way.

card.question: What is the farthest thing you can see with your own eyes?
card.glance: An elongated gray glow in Andromeda with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, the middle bright star of Andromeda, climb two fainter stars to the north and the glow appears. The oval core is obvious, and with averted vision the haze stretches about three degrees, six Moon widths, with M32 as a fuzzy “star” just south of the core.
card.understand: Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our Milky Way, seen steeply tilted, so its disk is squeezed into an oval. For centuries it was a “nebula” of unknown distance, until Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid in it in 1923, a pulsing star whose rhythm gives away its true brightness. How faint that star looked put Andromeda far outside our galaxy, and Hubble’s modern namesake telescope has since timed 55 of them.
card.answer: For most people it is this glow: hundreds of billions of suns whose light set out about 2.5 million years ago, before our species existed. You see the galaxy as it was when our ancestors were first shaping stone tools.
card.wonder: Andromeda is closing on us at about 300 km/s, and billions of years from now it and the Milky Way may merge into a single galaxy.
card.connect: Our own galaxy would look much like this from outside, with small companions of its own, like M32 here.

lens.beat: Cepheids in another galaxy
lens.question: Why did Hubble's first distance to Andromeda come out less than half the true value?
lens.why: The Andromeda Galaxy is where the pulsing-star ruler first left the Milky Way, and its history shows how every rung depends on the ones below.
lens.look: From Mirach climb two fainter stars to the north and the glow appears: an obvious oval core and, with averted vision, a haze stretching about three degrees. M32 is a fuzzy star just south of the core.
lens.answer: The calibration of the Cepheid rule available to Hubble at the time was off, so every distance it gave came out too small, and fixing the lower rungs later stretched Andromeda out to about 2.5 million light-years. The ladder you climbed tonight is the corrected one, and at its top stands a galaxy whose light left before our species existed.
lens.story: Hubble's method was sound: he found pulsing stars in photographs of Andromeda, timed their beats, read off their true power from Leavitt's rule and compared it with how faint they looked. The weak point was the rule's zero point, borrowed from pulsing stars in our own galaxy that, as Walter Baade showed in 1952, were an older and fainter kind than Andromeda's Cepheids.

journeys.title: Orion, One Record at a Time
journeys.drivingQuestion: How far up the sky's record book can plain starlight take you?
journeys.hook: Know a star's distance, and its light starts answering questions it used to hide.
journeys.story: Tonight's climb runs from single stars to whole crowds, where the record is written in time. Starting with the Hyades, each answer opens the next question, until M35 is dated by the stars it has already lost.
journeys.payoff: Tonight's ladder ended with time, where records are set in years and in numbers of stars rather than in brightness. A crowd is dated by the rule that heavy stars burn out first, so the richest and oldest are measured with the same physics as the single stars before them. The oldest of them formed when the galaxy was young, and their light is the nearest thing to a fossil that binoculars can show.

stops.name: Hyades

getThere.text: Find the Hyades by eye, the V of stars around orange Aldebaran in Taurus, about 60° up in the south-east. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: A cluster is a family whose members share one distance, so the nearest family of all is where stars of many kinds can be compared side by side at a known range.

card.question: How can a cluster’s colors tell its age?
card.glance: A big V of stars spilling past the edges of the field, several of them yellow-orange.
card.see: The V of the Bull’s face in Taurus is too big for one view, so sweep along each arm. A few cluster stars are tinted orange among the white ones. Aldebaran, the brightest orange point at one tip, is the odd one out.
card.understand: Because the Hyades are so close, the Hipparcos satellite could measure the parallax of individual members and map the cluster in three dimensions, with its core about 150 light-years away. The family is about 625 million years old, five times older than the Pleiades. In that time its heaviest blue stars have died, and the next heaviest have swollen into orange giants.
card.answer: The color of the brightest members is the clock: blue-white stars mean the heavy ones are still alive, while orange giants among white and yellow stars mean that era has passed.
card.wonder: Gaia has traced stars escaping from it into two long tails, one leading and one trailing the cluster along its orbit, each stretching for hundreds of light-years.
card.connect: The brightest star in the V, Aldebaran, does not belong to the family at all.

lens.beat: How far: the nearest star cluster
lens.question: How far away is the nearest star cluster, and why does that matter?
lens.why: A cluster is a family whose members share one distance, so the nearest family of all is where stars of many kinds can be compared side by side at a known range.
lens.look: The V of the Bull's face in Taurus is too big for one view, so sweep along each arm. Every family member you pass sits at nearly the same distance, which makes their differences in brightness and color real; Aldebaran, the bright orange star at one tip, lies in front and does not count.
lens.answer: The core of the Hyades lies about 150 light-years away, closer than any other true cluster, so its stars spill past the edges of your field. Because every member shares that distance, their differences in brightness are differences in real power, the number every later record rests on: how much light a star truly makes.
lens.story: Long before satellites, the Hyades gave up their distance through perspective. The members move through space in parallel, so their paths across the sky seem to converge on one point, the way railway tracks meet at the horizon, and the angle to that point, combined with each star's speed toward us read from its spectrum, turns a drift in arcseconds into a speed in kilometers per second. Set the two side by side and the distance falls out, and for most of the twentieth century this was the rung on which brighter, farther yardsticks were calibrated.

stops.name: Bellatrix
stops.role: How much light: the most powerful

getThere.text: Move down about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (17°), and Bellatrix is there, in Orion.

stops.whyHere: Bellatrix and Betelgeuse look nearly equal in brightness, and only their distances can say which one is working harder.
stops.transitionText: With a distance settled at the Hyades, a star's glow can finally be split into nearness and power, and at Bellatrix the power is what the glow was hiding.

card.question: Are Orion’s two shoulders neighbors in space?
card.glance: Orion’s western shoulder, a blue-white star opposite orange Betelgeuse.
card.see: Put Bellatrix in the field, then swing across to Betelgeuse: blue-white against orange. They look similar in brightness, yet they are very different stars at very different distances.
card.understand: Bellatrix is a hot blue-white star whose yearly parallax shift, measured by the Hipparcos satellite, puts it much closer than the Belt stars. A constellation is a pattern drawn on a flat sky. The stars that make it can lie at wildly different depths, like streetlights on different streets lining up when seen from one window.
card.answer: Bellatrix lies about 250 light-years away, roughly half as far as Betelgeuse, and only from Earth do the two line up into the shoulders of one hunter.
card.wonder: Seen from another star system, Orion’s outline would fall apart.
card.connect: Between the two shoulders runs a thermometer: blue-white is hot, orange is cool.

lens.beat: How much light: Orion's nearer shoulder
lens.question: Do Orion's two shoulders, so alike in brightness, make the same amount of light?
lens.why: Bellatrix and Betelgeuse look nearly equal in brightness, and only their distances can say which one is working harder.
lens.answer: They do not, for Bellatrix pours out about 7,000 times the Sun's light, while Betelgeuse, about twice as far, must make many times more to look as bright. Two stars can match in looks and differ widely in power, and whether that power comes from heat or from size is written in their colors, blue-white for one and orange for the other.
lens.story: Comparing two stars' power takes more than their distances. Betelgeuse sends much of its light out as infrared and Bellatrix much of its as ultraviolet, both invisible, so each visible glow has to be scaled up before the totals can be compared, and the corrections run in opposite directions.

stops.name: 15 Monocerotis
stops.role: How hot: the hottest and coolest

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the left about three fields of your 6.5° binoculars (19°) to 15 Monocerotis, in Monoceros.

stops.whyHere: The Christmas Tree Cluster's brightest star belongs to the hottest class there is, and the gap between its color and Betelgeuse's, on the way there, is a temperature gap you can see.
stops.transitionText: Bellatrix pours out a measured amount of light, but not how: a hotter surface shines more from every square meter, a bigger one has more of them, and the color of 15 Monocerotis reads the first.

card.question: What lights up the cloud around the Christmas Tree Cluster?
card.glance: The bright ‘trunk’ star of the Christmas Tree Cluster in Monoceros.
card.see: Sweep about 11° east of Betelgeuse to a small triangular group: the Christmas Tree Cluster, upside down, with 15 Mon as the bright star at its base. The Cone Nebula at the tree’s tip is for cameras only.
card.understand: 15 Monocerotis belongs to the hottest, heaviest class of stars, at the heart of the Christmas Tree Cluster, a family about five million years old. Gaia’s parallaxes for the cluster’s stars place the family about 2,300 light-years away, and models read its age from the colors and brightnesses of the members. Published temperatures for 15 Mon itself range widely, a reminder that a star wrapped in gas is hard to read.
card.answer: The cloud is lit by 15 Monocerotis itself, whose ultraviolet light makes the leftover gas glow and slowly eats into the dark cloud that holds the Cone Nebula, the way spring sunshine wears down a snowbank.
card.wonder: It is so luminous that it still shows to the naked eye from that distance under dark skies.
card.connect: In Orion’s Sword, a similar heavy star still sits deep inside its glowing nebula.

lens.beat: How hot: the hottest class of star
lens.question: How hot is the star at the foot of the Christmas Tree Cluster?
lens.why: The Christmas Tree Cluster's brightest star belongs to the hottest class there is, and the gap between its color and Betelgeuse's, on the way there, is a temperature gap you can see.
lens.look: Sweep about 11° east of Betelgeuse to the small, upside-down triangle of the Christmas Tree Cluster, with 15 Monocerotis as the bright star at its base. Compare its crisp white light with orange Betelgeuse on the way: the color gap between them is a temperature gap of tens of thousands of degrees.
lens.answer: Published values run from about 25,000 to 45,000 K, a reminder that even the thermometer has error bars when a star sits inside a cloud of its own glowing gas. Either way each square meter of it outshines the Sun's many times over, so its power needs far less surface than a cool star's would.
lens.story: For the hottest stars the thermometer is a balance between spectral lines. Helium that still holds both its electrons absorbs at some colors, helium stripped of one absorbs at others, and the hotter the surface, the more the stripped kind wins, so the ratio places a star on the scale. The same balance defines the hottest class itself, the O stars, and 15 Monocerotis is a member in good standing.

stops.name: Betelgeuse
stops.role: How big: the largest and smallest

getThere.text: From 15 Monocerotis, slide up and to the right about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (12°) to Betelgeuse, in Orion.

stops.whyHere: Orion's red shoulder is cool yet brilliant, exactly the mix that forces an enormous surface, and it is the size record most people know.
stops.transitionText: Color gave the temperature of 15 Monocerotis, and so how much light each square meter of a star sends out; divide a star's whole power by that, and you have the surface that gives Betelgeuse its width.

card.question: How can a star cooler than the Sun outshine almost everything around it?
card.glance: A bright orange-red star on Orion’s shoulder, whose color blooms when you nudge the focus slightly off.
card.see: Betelgeuse marks Orion’s eastern shoulder, the bright orange star opposite blue-white Rigel. Turn the focus a little past sharp and the point blooms into a small disk whose orange-red suddenly becomes obvious; swing to Rigel to feel the contrast. Its brightness drifts over months, so judge it fresh each time.
card.understand: A star’s color is a thermometer, and Betelgeuse’s says its surface is only about 3,600 K, well below the Sun’s 5,800 K, so each square meter of it shines more feebly than the Sun’s. The surprise is how many square meters there are. Astronomers timed its slow pulsations and fed them into models of how heavy stars age, and out came about 18 Suns’ worth of matter swollen to some 760 times the Sun’s width.
card.answer: That is the whole trick: a dim glow spread over an almost absurd amount of surface still adds up to far more light than the Sun will ever give.
card.wonder: Put Betelgeuse where the Sun is and its surface would reach past the orbit of Mars.
card.connect: Heavy stars like this do not fade quietly, and the wreckage of one that already exploded lies next door in Taurus.

lens.beat: How big: the most famous giant
lens.question: Is Betelgeuse the largest star you can see, or only the most famous?
lens.why: Orion's red shoulder is cool yet brilliant, exactly the mix that forces an enormous surface, and it is the size record most people know.
lens.answer: It is one of the largest the naked eye can reach, but not the champion: VY Canis Majoris, a binocular star in the Great Dog, is nearly twice as wide, and the Garnet Star may also be bigger. Like them, Betelgeuse is a heavy star swollen late in life, and because heavy stars burn out first, which of them a crowd still holds tells how old the crowd is.
lens.story: Betelgeuse was the first star beyond the Sun whose width was ever measured. In 1920 Albert Michelson and Francis Pease mounted a steel beam across the top of the great Mount Wilson telescope, with mirrors that could be slid apart along it, and watched the interference pattern vanish when the mirrors stood about three meters apart, the separation that matched the star's disk. Every size record since descends from that experiment.

stops.name: M35
stops.role: How old: the oldest stars and richest crowds

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (17°) to M35, in Gemini.

stops.whyHere: M35, at Gemini's feet, is young enough that its age has been read two ways, from the stars it has lost and from how fast its Sun-like stars still spin.
stops.transitionText: A size like that of Betelgeuse belongs to the late stages of a star's life, and heavy stars reach them first, which is why the stars a crowd like M35 has already lost tell how old it is.

card.question: Why does M35 look fainter than the Pleiades though they are the same age?
card.glance: A rich, glittering patch near Gemini’s feet, with many stars resolved and visible to the eye on a dark night.
card.see: Find Gemini’s feet, η and μ Geminorum, and move about two degrees north-west. M35 is a round, grainy glow sprinkled with resolved stars, about the size of the full Moon, and just south-west lies a much smaller smudge, NGC 2158.
card.understand: M35’s age was found in an unusual way. Young stars spin fast and slowly brake as they age, like a top winding down, so the rotation periods of hundreds of its Sun-like stars make a clock, and it reads about 150 million years, close to the Pleiades. Gaia counts about 1,600 members.
card.answer: It is a matter of distance, for at about six times the Pleiades’ distance only M35’s brightest stars show individually and the rest merge into a glow.
card.wonder: Reading a cluster's age from how fast its Sun-like stars spin gives the same answer as the older methods, which is why astronomers now trust that clock for lone stars like the Sun.
card.connect: The little smudge at its edge, NGC 2158, is not part of this family at all.

lens.beat: How old: the cluster at Gemini's feet
lens.question: How old is M35, and do two different clocks agree on it?
lens.why: M35, at Gemini's feet, is young enough that its age has been read two ways, from the stars it has lost and from how fast its Sun-like stars still spin.
lens.answer: Both clocks agree that it is a young crowd, a little older than the Pleiades: its heaviest blue stars are already gone, and its Sun-like stars have only begun to brake. With M35's stars at one known distance, each kind has a measured output, and the same kinds looking much fainter in NGC 2158 are one way that cluster's distance is read.
lens.story: The faint patch beside it, NGC 2158, looks like a junior companion but lies several times farther away and is roughly ten times older. Side by side they show the age rule at work: M35 still holds hot blue-white stars, while its old neighbor's brightest members have long since turned yellow and orange.

journeys.title: Finding Lyra's True Partners
journeys.drivingQuestion: How can two points of light end up weighing a star?
journeys.hook: Some pairs in the sky are partners in orbit, and some are strangers lined up by chance.
journeys.story: A double star may be partners in orbit or two stars that only share a line of sight, and only measurement says which. From Zeta Lyrae to the Double-Double the night follows that evidence, until a single point turns out to hold more partners than any binoculars can split.
journeys.payoff: Two points of light become a scale only when they are bound in orbit, and the night ended at the Double-Double, where bound stars crowd inside one point. Orbits like theirs, timed and measured, give the weights of the stars in them. Heavy stars almost never live alone, so the sky's brightest points are often its busiest, while the Sun, single and of unremarkable weight, is one of the quieter ways a star can live.

stops.name: Zeta Lyrae

getThere.text: Find Vega by eye, the brilliant blue-white star of Lyra, brightest of the Summer Triangle, about 60° up in the west. From there, hop up and to the left about 2° (a fraction of one field of your 6.5° binoculars) to Zeta Lyrae.

stops.whyHere: A star can only be weighed by a partner that circles it, so the hunt starts with the simplest discovery of all, that one point is two, and ζ Lyrae, a corner of Lyra's little parallelogram, makes it easy.

card.question: What makes a double star easy to split?
card.glance: A white star 2° south-east of Vega in Lyra that binoculars split into an unequal 44″ pair.
card.see: ζ Lyrae forms a small triangle with Vega and the Double-Double, at the top corner of Lyra's parallelogram. Binoculars show a brighter white star with a fainter companion just to the south-east.
card.understand: Two things decide a split: the gap and the difference in brightness. Here the gap is 44″, comfortably wide for binoculars though far tighter than the 3.5′ between the two halves of ε Lyrae next door. The companion is fainter but not overwhelmed, so it stands clear of the glare.
card.answer: A wide gap and a modest difference in brightness: ζ Lyrae's 44″ is easy for any binoculars, and its unequal pair makes the fainter star easy to pick out.
card.wonder: Its light left about 160 years ago, around the time the first telegraph cable across the Atlantic began carrying messages.
card.connect: Down the parallelogram lie red δ² Lyrae and variable Sheliak.

lens.beat: First split: an unequal pair
lens.question: Why does ζ Lyrae look single to the eye yet split in any binoculars?
lens.why: A star can only be weighed by a partner that circles it, so the hunt starts with the simplest discovery of all, that one point is two, and ζ Lyrae, a corner of Lyra's little parallelogram, makes it easy.
lens.look: ζ Lyrae makes a small triangle with Vega and the Double-Double. Binoculars split it into a white star with a fainter companion just to its south-east, clear at 10× and still separate at 7× if you hold steady.
lens.answer: That gap, around an eightieth of a degree, is one the unaided eye merges into a single point, while magnification spreads it into clear dark sky. Now there are two stars to question, and the split alone cannot say what they are or whether they are even near each other.
lens.story: William Herschel set out in the 1780s to use pairs like this one as rulers, assuming the fainter star lay far behind the brighter, so that the nearer star's yearly shift would betray its distance. He measured hundreds of pairs for about two decades and found something else: some of them were slowly turning around each other. In 1803 he announced that gravity binds stars in orbits just as it binds the planets, and a plan to measure distances had turned up the only scale that can weigh a star.

card.question: Can you see a star's temperature by comparing two neighbors?
card.glance: An orange-red 4th-magnitude star at the north-east corner of Lyra's parallelogram, with blue-white δ¹ nearby.

lens.question: What do the two colors of δ Lyrae say about its stars?

stops.name: Albireo

getThere.text: Sweep left about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (12°) to Albireo, in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: Albireo is the double that makes people fall for doubles, and for generations astronomers took it for granted that its gold and blue stars circle each other.
stops.transitionText: Colors told what the stars of δ² Lyrae are but not whether they belong together, so at Albireo the test turns to distance and motion, where many pretty pairs fail.

card.question: Can you really read a star's temperature from its color?
card.glance: The swan's head in Cygnus, roughly halfway from Vega to Altair; steady binoculars split it into gold and blue.
card.see: Albireo marks the head of the swan, at the foot of the Northern Cross. Brace your binoculars on something solid and at 10× it splits into a golden-orange star with a blue-white spark beside it, 34″ away; if the split is hard, let the image drift and watch for the blue point trailing behind.
card.understand: Think of an electric stove ring as it heats: first dull red, then orange, and, if it could get hot enough, white and then blue. card.answer: You can, and Albireo proves it: the golden star is only about a third as hot as its blue companion, and your eye registers that gap as color. Every tint you notice tonight is a surface temperature read across hundreds of light-years.
card.wonder: For a century Albireo was the textbook orbiting pair; precise Gaia-era motions now suggest two siblings born together and slowly drifting apart.
card.connect: The Double-Double near Vega shows pairs that truly do orbit each other.

lens.beat: Not a couple: siblings drifting apart
lens.question: Is Albireo, the sky's favorite gold-and-blue pair, really a couple in orbit?
lens.why: Albireo is the double that makes people fall for doubles, and for generations astronomers took it for granted that its gold and blue stars circle each other.
lens.look: Albireo marks the swan's head at the foot of the Northern Cross. Brace your binoculars and at 10× it splits into a golden-orange star with a blue-white companion about 34 arcseconds away. At 7× the blue star hugs the gold one, so let the image drift and watch for the blue point trailing behind.
lens.answer: The blue star is very unlikely to be bound to the gold one, so the pair the eye adores cannot weigh either star. The only orbit here hides inside the gold point, where a close companion circles it about every 121 years, a scale no binoculars can show.
lens.story: Settling it took more than a century of numbers: speeds toward us read from spectra, careful measurements of the gap, and finally the motions measured from space. In 2021 a team combined them all and found that the blue star's motion is very hard to fit to any orbit around the gold one, even though the two lie at about the same distance, roughly 400 light-years. A chance alignment of two such stars is wildly improbable, so the likeliest reading, though not a closed case, is two stars of one birth that have since slipped out of each other's grip.

stops.name: Sheliak

getThere.text: Move down and to the right about one and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (10°), and Sheliak is there, in Lyra.

stops.whyHere: Sheliak, at the bottom of Lyra, looks like an ordinary binocular double, but its brighter point hides a pair so close that the two stars touch, and they are among the sky's working scales.
stops.transitionText: Where Albireo turned out not to be a couple, Sheliak passes every test, two stars at one distance sharing one path, and that is what lets an orbit act as a scale.

card.question: Why does Sheliak fade and recover every 13 days, as regular as a clock?
card.glance: The western of the two stars at the bottom of Lyra, south of Vega; its brightness changes every few days.
card.see: Sheliak and Sulafat sit 2° apart at the bottom of Lyra, an ideal pair to compare. On some nights they look equal, while at the deepest eclipse Sheliak is clearly the fainter, so note which is brighter and check again a few nights later.
card.understand: We see this pair's orbit almost edge-on, so each star passes in front of the other in turn, an arrangement called an eclipsing binary. The two are so close that the light never settles: the lighter star has been stretched into a teardrop and spills gas onto its partner, which hides inside a thick disk of the stolen material. In 2008 the CHARA array imaged that teardrop directly.
card.answer: Two stars orbiting every 13 days keep stepping in front of each other while one feeds the other. So much gas changes hands that the orbit lengthens by about 19 seconds every year, a clock you can literally watch slowing down.
card.wonder: The heavier star, about 13 times the Sun's mass, is completely buried in its disk; we know it is there only by its pull.
card.connect: RR Lyrae, a few degrees away, dims for a different reason: the star itself breathes.

lens.beat: Partners: weighed by its eclipses
lens.question: How can two stars that no telescope can split be weighed?
lens.why: Sheliak, at the bottom of Lyra, looks like an ordinary binocular double, but its brighter point hides a pair so close that the two stars touch, and they are among the sky's working scales.
lens.look: Sheliak is the western of the two stars at the bottom of Lyra's parallelogram. At 10× a fainter companion stands about three-quarters of a minute of arc to the south-east, clear of the glare once you hold steady; at 7× it is a real test, so brace the binoculars firmly.
lens.answer: Their light does the weighing: the dips of the eclipses time the orbit, and the swing of the spectral lines gives the speeds and so the orbit's size. Together they weigh a donor of about three Suns feeding a far heavier partner, and the faint star in your binoculars may or may not belong, since its link has never been established.
lens.story: Most orbits are seen at a slant, and a spectrum alone cannot say how steep, which leaves every mass read from it uncertain. A pair whose stars eclipse each other has to be seen almost edge-on, so that unknown disappears. That is why eclipsing pairs are the sky's most trusted scales, even when the two stars are far too close for any telescope to split.

stops.name: Double-Double
stops.plainClass: four white stars in two pairs

getThere.text: Sweep right about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (6°) to the Double-Double, still in Lyra.

stops.whyHere: The Double-Double, a modest point beside Vega, breaks into two in binoculars, and that is only the first of its layers.
stops.transitionText: Sheliak showed one proven partnership; at the Double-Double the partnerships nest, pairs inside pairs within a single point of light.

card.question: How many stars can hide inside one faint point of light?
card.glance: Two matching white stars about 1.7° north-east of Vega in Lyra; any binoculars split them.
card.see: Put Vega at the edge of the field and look about 1.7° to the north-east: two matched white stars sit side by side like distant headlights. Very sharp eyes can see them as one slightly stretched star without optics, and any binoculars split them easily.
card.understand: Point a telescope at high power on either star and it splits again, into a pair a couple of arcseconds apart (an arcsecond is a 3,600th of a degree). Both close pairs lie at the same distance, about 158 light-years, and drift across the sky together, which would be a strange coincidence for strangers. Over centuries each pair circles its own balance point, and timing orbits like these is how astronomers weigh stars.
card.answer: Binoculars show two, a telescope shows four, and the shared distance and motion say all four form one family held together by gravity, so the dim point beside Vega is really a small stellar neighborhood.
card.wonder: The close pairs are about a hundred times tighter than the wide one, a system within a system.
card.connect: Two degrees south, Sheliak's two stars are packed so tightly they almost touch.

lens.beat: A crowd: four stars in two pairs
lens.question: How many stars are hiding in the little point beside Vega?
lens.why: The Double-Double, a modest point beside Vega, breaks into two in binoculars, and that is only the first of its layers.
lens.look: Put Vega at the edge of the field and look about 1.7 degrees to the north-east: two matched white stars sit side by side about three and a half minutes of arc apart, split at any magnification. Neither half shows anything more in binoculars, however steady you hold them.
lens.answer: There are four suns in two close pairs, each pair certainly bound and slowly tracing an orbit that will one day give its weight. The wide link between the pairs turns so slowly that its speed is still hard to measure, so the claim that all four form one system rests on their shared distance and drift.
lens.story: Gravity tolerates crowds only in tiers. Three or four stars at similar distances from one another cannot stay together for long, because their pulls keep changing until one is flung out. A system lasts when it is built from close pairs that keep far apart from each other. Two tight pairs, each circling on its own while the pair of pairs wheels slowly around a common center, is that architecture in its plainest form.

journeys.title: Cygnus' Cradles and Graves
journeys.drivingQuestion: How can one night's sky show the whole life of a star?
journeys.hook: A star's life is far too long to watch, so we read it from many stars of different ages.
journeys.story: Every star you will see tonight is at a different moment of the same life, and the stops run in the order a star lives them, right through to its death. Weight is the thread: the heavier a star, the faster it travels that road and the more violently it ends.
journeys.payoff: From IC 1396 and Trumpler 37 to the Dumbbell Nebula you have followed one life by reading many, all the way to its end, with weight setting how fast each star lived. The end hands a star's matter back to the clouds, enriched with carbon and other elements it forged, and the Dumbbell Nebula is one such gift on its way back. In time it will be gathered into a new nursery, the same road that the material of the Sun and the Earth once took.
journeys.difficultyReason: IC 1396 and Trumpler 37 is faint or tricky to find.

stops.name: IC 1396 and Trumpler 37
stops.plainClass: glowing gas cloud where stars form

getThere.text: Find Alderamin by eye, the brightest star of Cepheus, about 65° up in the north. From there, hop up and to the right about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (6°) to IC 1396 and Trumpler 37.

stops.whyHere: Every star begins in a cloud, and in IC 1396 a young cluster and the cold gas around it share one field, the raw material and the first results side by side.

card.question: Can one generation of stars trigger the birth of the next?
card.glance: A loose cluster around a star at the naked-eye limit, south of the Garnet Star in Cepheus, inside a huge faint nebula.
card.see: Put the deep-orange Garnet Star at the north edge of the field; about 1.5° south-south-west a scatter of stars gathers around a brighter one, HD 206267. Under a dark sky a faint glow may surround it, but expect stars rather than the pink cloud of photographs.
card.understand: The central star is really a group of very hot, heavy stars whose ultraviolet light makes the surrounding hydrogen glow. Where their light and winds squeeze the edges of the cloud, the gas is pressed dense enough for gravity to take over and collapse it into new stars. Infrared telescopes, which see through dust, found protostars less than a million years old inside the dark “Elephant’s Trunk” at the nebula’s edge, younger than the stars squeezing them.
card.answer: It can, and in IC 1396 the light and winds of hot young stars are pressing the edges of their cloud into new stars right now. Different corners of the cluster have different ages, a record of star birth spreading in waves.
card.wonder: In a few million years the heaviest stars here will swell into red supergiants like the Garnet Star at the edge of your field.
card.connect: NGC 7160, just to the north, shows the same family’s older generation, its birth cloud already gone.

lens.beat: Nursery: one generation sparks the next
lens.question: How much of the cloud at IC 1396's edge is actually turning into stars?
lens.why: Every star begins in a cloud, and in IC 1396 a young cluster and the cold gas around it share one field, the raw material and the first results side by side.
lens.look: Start at the Garnet Star and move about a degree and a half south-south-west to the scatter of stars around HD 206267. That bright central star is the group of hot stars doing the work; the glowing gas they press on is faint at best in binoculars.
lens.answer: So far only about five percent of the mass of the dark globule called the Elephant's Trunk has turned into protostars. Much of the rest will be boiled away by the hot stars' light before it can collapse, which is why clouds make stars so wastefully, and why their families soon find themselves standing in the open.
lens.story: The hot stars at the center are pushing a front of compressed gas into the cloud around them, and new stars form where that front arrives. Inside the Elephant's Trunk the young stars grow younger the deeper they lie in the globule, the pattern expected if the squeeze is moving inward and setting off collapse as it goes.

stops.name: M39

getThere.text: Sweep up about one and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (9°) to M39, in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: M39 is a family close enough for you to count its brightest members one by one.
stops.transitionText: The stars born in clouds like IC 1396 and Trumpler 37 will one day travel together as a family like M39, long after their birth gas has vanished.

card.question: How many stars of a nearby family can you count one by one?
card.glance: A large, bright, loose triangle of a few dozen stars north-east of Deneb, easy in any binoculars.
card.see: From Deneb, sweep about 9° east-north-east in Cygnus to a loose triangle of stars about the size of the full Moon, standing out from the Milky Way. At your lowest power count the members, and notice that the brightest are all white or blue-white.
card.understand: Gaia shows these stars sharing one distance, about 965 light-years, and one motion through space: an open cluster, a family born together. A 2024 study of their spectra fits an age of roughly 430 million years, though another method gives a third of that, a reminder that cluster ages depend on models. The bluest heavyweights have burned out, and the brightest survivors are white stars of about three solar masses.
card.answer: You can count a few dozen, M39's brightest white stars standing out one by one, the visible tip of a family Gaia counts at over five hundred.
card.wonder: Aristotle may have noted it as a comet-like smudge around 325 BC, which would make it one of the first star clusters ever written down.
card.connect: NGC 6819, deeper in Cygnus, is several times older and has somehow held together.

lens.beat: A family in its middle years
lens.question: What happens to M39's family as its stars age?
lens.why: M39 is a family close enough for you to count its brightest members one by one.
lens.answer: It ages from the top down. Its brightest white stars are the next in line to spend their core hydrogen and swell into giants, and as each one does, the family's light grows a little fainter and warmer, just as it did when its bluest members burned out long ago.

resolved.question: What happens to M39's family as its stars age?
resolved.transition: The stars born in clouds like IC 1396 and Trumpler 37 will one day travel together as a family like M39, long after their birth gas has vanished.
resolved.why: M39 is a family close enough for you to count its brightest members one by one.
resolved.look: From Deneb, sweep about 9° east-north-east in Cygnus to a loose triangle of stars about the size of the full Moon, standing out from the Milky Way. At your lowest power count the members, and notice that the brightest are all white or blue-white.
resolved.understand: Gaia shows these stars sharing one distance, about 965 light-years, and one motion through space: an open cluster, a family born together. A 2024 study of their spectra fits an age of roughly 430 million years, though another method gives a third of that, a reminder that cluster ages depend on models. The bluest heavyweights have burned out, and the brightest survivors are white stars of about three solar masses.
resolved.answer: It ages from the top down. Its brightest white stars are the next in line to spend their core hydrogen and swell into giants, and as each one does, the family's light grows a little fainter and warmer, just as it did when its bluest members burned out long ago.
resolved.wonder: Aristotle may have noted it as a comet-like smudge around 325 BC, which would make it one of the first star clusters ever written down.

stops.name: Deneb

getThere.text: Move up and to the left about one and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (9°), and Deneb is there, still in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: Deneb is a heavyweight whose old age is happening fast.
stops.transitionText: Every member of a family like M39 will one day run out of core hydrogen and swell, and Deneb is a star that has already reached that stage.

card.question: Why does the most powerful star of the Summer Triangle look the faintest?
card.glance: The faintest corner of the Summer Triangle, the swan's tail in Cygnus, set in a rich Milky Way field.
card.see: Deneb marks the tail of Cygnus, the swan, and the top of the Northern Cross. Sweep slowly around it and the field fills with countless faint stars, because here you are looking along the Milky Way; then glance back at Vega, which is plainly brighter to the eye.
card.understand: Vega is about 25 light-years away. Deneb is too far for a precise parallax, so its distance is still argued over, but the best estimate puts it around 2,600 light-years, roughly a hundred times farther. Light thins out with the square of distance, so a star a hundred times farther must pour out ten thousand times more light just to keep up.
card.answer: Deneb only looks modest because it is so far away. It is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen to about 200 times the Sun's width and shining with something like 200,000 Suns, and even from that distance it nearly keeps pace with its neighbor.
card.wonder: If the best estimate is right, the light entering your eye tonight set out when Rome was still a small kingdom.
card.connect: Stars like Deneb do not stay white: the Garnet Star in Cepheus shows the red supergiant stage that lies ahead.

lens.beat: Aging supergiant on its way to red
lens.question: What is Deneb turning into?
lens.why: Deneb is a heavyweight whose old age is happening fast.
lens.look: Deneb is the bright white star at the tail of the swan, the top of the Northern Cross. Its white is the color of a heavyweight only partway to red; sweep about 16° north-north-east into Cepheus to the Garnet Star, a deep orange-red supergiant at the stage Deneb is heading for.
lens.answer: Deneb is most likely turning into a red supergiant. Its surface already shows nitrogen dredged up from the core, a sign that it has burned through its core hydrogen, and the best models have it swelling toward the red supergiant stage on its way to a supernova. For now it is a white star about 200 times the Sun's width, midway through that crossing.
lens.story: A heavy star burns hydrogen through a cycle that uses carbon as a go-between and turns much of it into nitrogen, so nitrogen showing up at the surface means material from the core has been mixed outward. In Deneb that mixing is strong enough to measure, one of the main clues that the star has finished its core hydrogen rather than still being in its prime.

stops.name: P Cygni

getThere.text: Move left about one and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (8°), and P Cygni is there, still in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: P Cygni is a heavyweight so luminous that it is already coming apart at the seams.
stops.transitionText: Deneb still has a long stretch of old age ahead, while P Cygni has almost nothing left to burn and is already letting its outer layers slip away.

card.question: What happens when a star is almost too heavy to hold itself together?
card.glance: A modest 5th-magnitude star about 2½° south-west of Sadr, the center of the Northern Cross in Cygnus.
card.see: From Sadr, at the center of the Northern Cross, slide about 2½° south-west toward Albireo. P Cygni is a plain white point against the Milky Way, easy in binoculars, and nothing in the view hints at its power.
card.understand: P Cygni is a luminous blue variable, one of the heaviest and most luminous kinds of star. In a star this bright the outflowing light itself pushes on the gas almost as hard as gravity pulls it back, so the outer layers are barely held. It leaks mass in a fierce wind and now and then lets go of much more at once; the 1600 eruption threw off a shell that is still expanding today.
card.answer: It starts to come apart: light nearly overpowers gravity, and the star sheds itself in a steady wind and sudden outbursts like the one of 1600. Its name lives on in the P Cygni profile, the spectral signature astronomers use to spot any star blowing a wind.
card.wonder: It still looks this bright from over five thousand light-years away.
card.connect: WR 136, just over a degree away, has already blown off its outer layers.

lens.beat: On the brink: a star blowing itself apart
lens.question: How will P Cygni's struggle against its own light end?
lens.why: P Cygni is a heavyweight so luminous that it is already coming apart at the seams.
lens.answer: It will end with its core collapsing, after it has lost much more of itself. Its winds and outbursts strip away mass, like the shell of about a tenth of a Sun it threw off in 1600, and when the core has burned through its last fuel it will fall in on itself, most likely in a supernova.

stops.name: Dumbbell Nebula
stops.role: The end: what a star leaves behind

getThere.text: From P Cygni, slide down and to the left about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (16°) to the Dumbbell Nebula, in Vulpecula.

stops.whyHere: The Dumbbell is what a star like the Sun leaves when it is done, close enough that binoculars show its shape on a dark, moonless night.
stops.transitionText: P Cygni has its ending still ahead, and the Dumbbell Nebula shows what one kind of ending leaves behind.

card.question: Where is the easiest place to see how a Sun-like star dies?
card.glance: A small gray patch, clearly larger than any star, sometimes with a hint of a pinched apple-core shape.
card.see: Find the little arrow of Sagitta below Albireo, then move about 3° north of its tip star, γ Sagittae, into Vulpecula. The Dumbbell is a small, faint gray smudge; brace the binoculars and look slightly to one side, and on a dark night it turns squarish or hourglass-shaped.
card.understand: A star once like the Sun swelled into a giant and let its outer layers drift away, and its bare, extremely hot core now makes that gas glow like a neon sign. The outer shells are expanding at about 30 kilometers per second, and dividing the shell's size by that speed gives an age of roughly ten thousand years. Within tens of thousands more the gas will fade into space, carrying elements made inside the star.
card.answer: The Dumbbell may be the best place of all: a Sun-like star's shed layers, lit by its bare core and close enough, about 1,270 light-years, to show their shape in binoculars.
card.wonder: Its outer gas moves fast enough to cross the United States in under three minutes, yet from here the shape will look unchanged for your whole lifetime.
card.connect: Heavier stars go out violently; the Veil in Cygnus is the wreck of such an explosion.

image.license: CC BY 4.0
image.caption: Large-telescope composite: colors and the full hourglass the eye cannot see in binoculars.

lens.beat: The end: a cast-off shell
lens.question: Is the Dumbbell the end of a star's story or a new beginning?
lens.why: The Dumbbell is what a star like the Sun leaves when it is done, close enough that binoculars show its shape on a dark, moonless night.
lens.answer: The Dumbbell is both. The white dwarf at its center will cool for billions of years and never shine by fusion again. But the gas, carrying elements made inside the star, will spread into the Galaxy's clouds, where future stars and planets will form from it, just as the Sun and Earth formed from material like this.
lens.story: The star at the Dumbbell's center is one of the hottest known, around a hundred thousand degrees, because it is the bare core that once burned helium deep inside the giant. Its ultraviolet light strips electrons from the gas around it, and as the core cools over the next tens of thousands of years the shell will dim until the glow goes out.

journeys.title: The Star Families of Perseus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Are stars born alone, or into families?
journeys.hook: The Sun lost its siblings long ago, and tonight's star families show how that happens.
journeys.story: Somewhere in the galaxy the Sun's brothers and sisters are still out there, scattered beyond recognition. Tonight's families show how that happens, from clusters still holding together to siblings strewn across the sky, recognized only by their motions.
journeys.payoff: Families of stars do not die so much as dissolve, and the last stop tonight showed that ending under way: siblings drifting apart, kin only by birth and by motion. The same thing happened to the Sun's family billions of years ago, so the Sun, too, is a scattered sibling, one star among many whose kin are spread around the galaxy. Gaia is already tracing such scattered families across the sky, families that dissolved long ago but still travel as one.
journeys.difficultyReason: Heart Nebula cluster is faint or tricky to find.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-east, around Perseus

stops.name: Heart Nebula cluster
stops.plainClass: newborn cluster still inside its cloud

getThere.text: Find Ruchbah by eye, a star of the W of Cassiopeia, about 70° up in the north. From there, hop down and to the right about one and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (8°) to the Heart Nebula cluster.

stops.whyHere: The cluster at the heart of the Heart Nebula is a family so young that it is still inside the cloud that made it, and its biggest siblings are already reshaping that cloud.

card.question: How do newborn stars make the cloud around them glow?
card.glance: A loose little group of stars in a rich Milky Way field of Cassiopeia, inside a nebula that belongs to photographs.
card.see: Sweep about five degrees east-south-east of Segin, the eastern end of Cassiopeia’s W, for a small, loose group of a dozen faint stars. Under a very dark sky a nebula filter may show a hint of glow; without one, expect only the stars.
card.understand: These stars are three or four million years old, and a handful are O stars, the hottest and heaviest kind, dozens of times the Sun’s mass. Their ultraviolet light tears electrons off the hydrogen atoms around them, and when an atom recaptures an electron it gives off light at particular colors, most strongly a deep red. Photographs show that glow sculpted into a heart, and within a few million years the stars’ winds will blow the cloud away.
card.answer: The newborns’ ultraviolet light keeps breaking the hydrogen apart, and each time the pieces rejoin they glow, like a neon sign powered by starlight. The Heart Nebula is that glow, shaped by the stars inside it.
card.wonder: When its stars switched on, our ancestors were already walking the Earth on two legs.
card.connect: The Double Cluster, nearby, shows what such a family looks like about ten million years further on.

image.caption: Survey photograph of the Heart Nebula's central cluster.

lens.beat: Born together: newborns in their cloud
lens.question: What do the heaviest newborns of a star family do to their own nest?
lens.why: The cluster at the heart of the Heart Nebula is a family so young that it is still inside the cloud that made it, and its biggest siblings are already reshaping that cloud.
lens.look: Sweep east-south-east of Segin, the eastern end of Cassiopeia's W, for a loose group of a dozen faint stars. A nebula filter may add a hint of glow under a very dark sky; without one you see only the family itself.
lens.answer: They light it up and then drive it away, and once the gas is gone the gravity holding the siblings together drops sharply. This cluster is the core of a much wider association of young stars, a sign of how loosely newborn families are tied.
lens.story: Whether a young family will hold together can be tested by weighing it with its own motions. If its members swarm faster than the visible mass can restrain, the family is already unbound and drifting apart, and measurements of this kind in many young groups find exactly that: most are expanding outward from where they formed. Gaia has even timed some of that expansion, running the motions back to the moment the stars were closest together.

stops.name: Double Cluster (h Persei)

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars: the Double Cluster (h Persei) is already in the same view, just above the Heart Nebula cluster.

stops.whyHere: h Persei is about the cleanest picture of a star family the sky offers: hundreds of stars from one cloud and one burst, still packed tightly enough to look like what they are.
stops.transitionText: Like the Heart Nebula cluster, the Double Cluster is a family whose members are still together, so take in what the two share before time starts to change them.

card.question: Why do a few orange stars shine among the Double Cluster’s blue-white crowd?
card.glance: Two rich swarms of stars side by side in one view between Cassiopeia and Perseus, a naked-eye smudge from a dark site.
card.see: Sweep from Cassiopeia’s W toward Perseus and two glittering knots appear in one field, each crowded with dozens of points, the western one, h Persei, a little richer in the middle. Look for a few orange stars among the blue-white, especially toward the eastern cluster.
card.understand: Both clusters formed in the same burst of star birth, so all their stars share a birthday. Most are hot blue-white stars many times heavier than the Sun, and the orange points are the heaviest of all. Weight is destiny for a star: the more massive it is, the faster it burns, so those few have already raced to their last chapter.
card.answer: The orange stars were born with the rest, but being the heaviest they aged fastest and have swollen into red supergiants, cool on the surface and orange in color. Their ages, read from the supergiants alone, match the cluster’s, a neat cross-check.
card.wonder: They lie about 7,400 light-years away, more than ten times farther than the Pleiades, yet are still bright enough to see without binoculars.
card.connect: Its twin, χ Persei, sits half a degree east, born of the same cloud at the same time.

lens.beat: Born together: twin litters
lens.question: What makes a few hundred points of light one family rather than a crowd?
lens.why: h Persei is about the cleanest picture of a star family the sky offers: hundreds of stars from one cloud and one burst, still packed tightly enough to look like what they are.
lens.look: Keep both halves of the Double Cluster in one field and settle on h Persei, the western knot, a little richer in the middle. Dozens of blue-white points crowd together, nearly all of one color, and that sameness is the first clue to a shared origin.
lens.answer: What makes them one is a shared birth, which astronomers can test: the members' parallaxes put them all at one distance, and the clocks read from different kinds of member all land near 14 million years. Its twin χ Persei and a wider halo of stars around both share that birthday, so this family even has cousins.
lens.story: The two cores are only the densest part of the family. Around them spreads a crowd of thousands of stars with the same age and motion, reaching tens of light-years out, and studies of their motions suggest that the cores are bound while much of the outer crowd is not. The Double Cluster is therefore a family caught between two fates, part of it built to last and part already on its way out.

stops.name: Alpha Persei Cluster

getThere.text: From the Double Cluster (h Persei), slide right about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (13°) to the Alpha Persei Cluster, still in Perseus.

stops.whyHere: The Alpha Persei Cluster is a family so near that it fills the whole binocular field, and its brightest member stands apart from its siblings in color as well as in brightness.
stops.transitionText: A family shares a birthday but not a lifespan, and at the Alpha Persei Cluster that difference has started to show.

card.question: What does a star family look like from up close?
card.glance: A loose spray of bright blue-white stars around yellow-white Mirfak, filling the whole field.
card.see: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus, and dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains. It is too big for most telescopes to frame, so binoculars or the eye alone take it in whole.
card.understand: This is an open cluster, a family of stars born together from one cloud, and Gaia picks out its members by their shared motion, like spotting a family walking together through a crowd. Its age comes from a subtle clue: the lightest members slowly destroy the lithium inside them, so the line between stars that still have lithium and those that have lost it works like a clock. Here it reads about 90 million years.
card.answer: Like the Alpha Persei Cluster: at 566 light-years its members spread over several Moon widths, a spray only binoculars can frame. Farther away, the same family would shrink into a small knot.
card.wonder: This family was born while dinosaurs still had tens of millions of years left.
card.connect: The Double Cluster, more than ten times farther away, shows how small a star family looks from across the galaxy.

lens.beat: First to age: Mirfak, the family's eldest
lens.question: Why does Mirfak look yellower than the blue-white siblings around it?
lens.why: The Alpha Persei Cluster is a family so near that it fills the whole binocular field, and its brightest member stands apart from its siblings in color as well as in brightness.
lens.look: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus, and dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains across the field. Compare Mirfak's tint with theirs: it is a shade yellower than any of its siblings.
lens.answer: Mirfak was born the heaviest of the family, so it burned through its core hydrogen first and swelled into a supergiant, its surface cooling to yellow-white while its lighter siblings stay blue-white in their prime. Born on the same day, they are reading different pages of the same life, and Mirfak is several chapters ahead.
lens.story: Mirfak is also a test of how well we understand aging stars. The family's lithium clock and the age implied by Mirfak's own size and temperature do not agree perfectly, and since the family's age is the sturdier figure, the gap points to physics the models have not quite captured, perhaps how heavy stars mix their cores or the spin they were born with. A family whose eldest has already turned is a laboratory for exactly that question.

stops.name: NGC 1582

getThere.text: From the Alpha Persei Cluster, slide down and to the right about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (13°) to NGC 1582, still in Perseus.

stops.whyHere: NGC 1582 is not especially old, but it is a weak family, small and spread wide, and it shows that thinning out is not only a matter of time.
stops.transitionText: Once the heaviest siblings have aged, as at the Alpha Persei Cluster, the next test is for the family as a whole, and NGC 1582 shows how a family fares against the galaxy's steady pull.

card.question: What does a star cluster look like as it dissolves?
card.glance: A broad, loose pattern of faint stars at the Perseus–Auriga border, with no bright center.
card.see: From ε Aurigae, the star beside Capella, sweep about five degrees west into Perseus. Look for a loose sprinkle of faint stars spread across more than half a degree.
card.understand: With only about 200 members spread wide, NGC 1582 has little gravity to hold itself together. Every pass near a gas cloud and every tug of the galaxy pulls a few more stars away. Gaia can still identify the family because its stars keep moving in the same direction, like a crowd leaving a stadium.
card.answer: It looks like NGC 1582, a thin sprinkle with no center, its members drifting off one by one into the Milky Way. The Sun was probably born in a family like this, long since dissolved.
card.wonder: Its light left about 3,100 years ago, around when the Phoenicians were spreading their alphabet.
card.connect: Compact NGC 1528 nearby is the contrast.

lens.beat: Thinning out: a family dissolving
lens.question: Was the Sun born into a family as loose as NGC 1582?

lens.answer: It may have been, though the Sun's family was probably a little bigger. Most star families are born small and loose, and NGC 1582, at about 135 million years, is already drifting apart member by member, the fate the Sun's own family met so long ago that its siblings are now spread around the galaxy.
lens.story: The Sun's birth family left clues in meteorites. The oldest grains in them once held radioactive atoms that decay within a few million years, so those atoms must have been made shortly before the solar system formed, most likely by heavy stars nearby, which suggests the Sun was born in a family rich enough to include such stars. That family has long since scattered, and astronomers now look for its members by matching chemistry, star by star.

stops.name: AE Aurigae

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the right about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (13°) to AE Aurigae, in Auriga.

stops.whyHere: AE Aurigae looks like an ordinary faint star near M38, but it was born in Orion, and it shows the most dramatic way a family can lose a member.
stops.transitionText: Where NGC 1582 still holds its family together, at least in part, AE Aurigae belongs to one whose members are scattered across the sky and tied together only by the way they move.

card.question: How did a star born in Orion end up in Auriga?
card.glance: A plain-looking star in Auriga, easy in binoculars, with a remarkable past.
card.see: Start at the star cluster M38 in Auriga and drift about 3° west-south-west to the lone brighter star there. Nothing about it looks unusual; the Flaming Star Nebula it lights up is a target for cameras.
card.understand: Stars drift slowly across the sky, and satellites measure that drift precisely. Run AE Aurigae’s motion backward and it meets another runaway, μ Columbae, which is racing the opposite way. Both paths converge on the young Trapezium cluster in Orion about 2.5 million years ago, and at the same spot sits a third suspect: ι Orionis, a tight pair of heavy stars on a stretched orbit.
card.answer: A close encounter between two pairs of heavy stars threw it out, sending AE Aurigae one way and μ Columbae the other like billiard balls after the break, and leaving ι Orionis behind as the battered survivor.
card.wonder: The Flaming Star Nebula that it lights up is not its birth cloud at all, just one it happens to be plowing through.
card.connect: Its birthplace, the Orion Nebula, is still making stars like it tonight.
