lens.beat: Scattered: a sibling thrown out
lens.question: How far can a star travel from its family in two and a half million years?
lens.why: AE Aurigae looks like an ordinary faint star near M38, but it was born in Orion, and it shows the most dramatic way a family can lose a member.
lens.look: From M38 drift about three degrees west-south-west to the lone, brighter star there. Nothing in the view marks it as unusual; its family tie is written entirely in its motion.
lens.answer: It can cross a good part of the sky. Flung out of the Orion Nebula's young cluster at high speed, AE Aurigae has covered hundreds of light-years and now shines among the stars of Auriga, far from any sibling. Its partner in flight, μ Columbae, left at the same moment in the opposite direction.
lens.story: Stars are thrown out of families in two ways. In one, a heavy partner explodes and its companion, suddenly released, flies off at its orbital speed; in the other, a close encounter among several stars in a crowded young cluster flings one outward while the rest tighten into a closer pair. AE Aurigae is the textbook case of the second kind, because the tightened pair it left behind can still be found in Orion's Sword.

journeys.title: How Perseus Fools the Eye
journeys.drivingQuestion: What can your eyes really tell you about a star, and where do they mislead?
journeys.hook: Your eye gets two clues from every star, brightness and color, and only one is honest.
journeys.story: Every star hands your eye two clues, how bright it looks and what color it is, and they do not deserve equal trust. Starting at Alfirk, each stop sets a star beside a neighbor, and the night ends among stars born together, where the same clues show which siblings have aged fastest.
journeys.payoff: Brightness misled, because it mixes a star's true power with its distance, while color held up as an honest thermometer of a star's surface. At Mirfak, among stars born together at one distance, the two clues read side by side pointed to the deepest difference of all, weight. The heaviest siblings burn their fuel fastest, so they are the first to swell and turn gold or red. Next time a cluster's stars look alike, look for the one whose color does not match, because it is telling you the family's age.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north, around Perseus

stops.name: Alfirk

getThere.text: Find Alderamin by eye, the brightest star of Cepheus, about 50° up in the north-west. From there, hop right about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (8°) to Alfirk.

stops.whyHere: Alfirk sits partway up the house of Cepheus from Alderamin, its bright corner, and beside that neighbor it looks like the lesser star, the kind of judgment the eye makes without thinking.

card.question: Can a star pulse every few hours without anyone noticing?
card.glance: A blue-white star in Cepheus that pulses every four and a half hours, too gently for your eyes.
card.see: β Cephei lies in Cepheus between Alderamin and Errai, and binoculars show a blue-white point. Its faint companion, 13.5 arcseconds away, needs a small telescope.
card.understand: Deep in β Cep’s layers, iron atoms trap heat when squeezed and release it when they expand, and that valve keeps the star ringing like a bell. The ringing shows up as a rhythm in its light and in the speed of its surface. Its light changes by only a few hundredths of a magnitude.
card.answer: It can, and for most of history nobody noticed, since β Cephei rings every 4.57 hours too faintly for any eye.
card.wonder: Alfirk rings like a bell several times a day, and astronomers read that ringing the way seismologists read earthquakes, to probe the hidden inside of a hot star.
card.connect: δ Cephei, in the same constellation, pulses slowly and deeply enough to follow by eye.

lens.beat: Fainter, farther, mightier
lens.question: Alderamin, the brightest star of Cepheus, outshines Alfirk; is it also the more powerful?
lens.why: Alfirk sits partway up the house of Cepheus from Alderamin, its bright corner, and beside that neighbor it looks like the lesser star, the kind of judgment the eye makes without thinking.
lens.look: Put Alderamin, the brightest star of Cepheus, in the field and then move to Alfirk, nearly a magnitude fainter and a little bluer. Both look like ordinary points, and nothing in their light says how far each has traveled.
lens.answer: Alderamin looks the stronger only because it is near, about 49 light-years away against Alfirk's 685, while Alfirk pours out about a thousand times more energy, roughly 19,000 Suns against 18. The brighter-looking star is simply the closer one, and nothing in either point of light hints at that until someone measures how far each lies.
lens.story: A hot star hides much of its power from the eye, because most of its energy comes out as ultraviolet, beyond violet, where we see nothing at all. Alfirk's visible glow is only a fraction of its true output, so here brightness misleads twice, once through distance and once through light the eye cannot catch.

stops.name: Garnet Star

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (12°) to the Garnet Star, still in Cepheus.

stops.whyHere: Cepheus holds one of the reddest stars visible without optics, set among white neighbors, and that contrast in color is a measurement you make the moment the star enters the field.
stops.transitionText: Brightness at Alfirk could not be read without a distance, so at the Garnet Star you turn to the clue that distance leaves alone, the color of a star.

card.question: How big can a star grow, and why does the Garnet Star glow so red?
card.glance: A deep orange-red point at the edge of the Milky Way in Cepheus, one of the reddest stars you can see without optics.
card.see: Start at Alderamin, the brightest star of Cepheus, and look toward ζ Cephei; the Garnet Star sits a little south of the halfway point. In binoculars its color leaps out against the white stars around it, and a slightly soft focus deepens it toward the gem it is named for.
card.understand: Heat a poker and it glows red, then orange, then white, and stars follow the same rule. At about 3,700 K the Garnet Star’s surface is far cooler than the Sun’s, yet the star is visible from more than a thousand light-years away. A cool surface can only pour out that much light if it is enormous, and interferometers, which combine telescopes to measure its tiny disk, confirm it.
card.answer: It is a red supergiant, swollen to roughly a thousand times the Sun’s width near the end of its life, and its cool surface glows deep orange. Dust in front of it reddens it further, the way haze reddens a setting Sun.
card.wonder: Set it in the Sun’s place and its surface would lie far beyond the orbit of Mars, perhaps out toward Jupiter.
card.connect: A star this heavy will end as a supernova, scattering the elements it forged, as Betelgeuse in Orion will.

lens.beat: The reddest ember
lens.question: What does the Garnet Star's deep red tell you that its brightness cannot?
lens.why: Cepheus holds one of the reddest stars visible without optics, set among white neighbors, and that contrast in color is a measurement you make the moment the star enters the field.
lens.look: From Alderamin, the brightest star of Cepheus, look toward ζ Cephei; the Garnet Star sits a little south of halfway. In binoculars its deep orange-red leaps out against the white stars around it, and a slightly soft focus strengthens it.
lens.answer: Its color reads a surface some two thousand degrees cooler than the Sun's, and that reading holds even though its distance is still argued over. What the color cannot do is weigh how much of that cool surface there is, which is the part that decides how much light the star truly gives.
lens.story: Astronomers turn the eye's impression into a number by measuring a star's brightness twice, once through a blue filter and once through a yellow one. The gap between the two, its color index, is about 2.35 magnitudes here, among the largest of any star you can see unaided, and a little of that is dust along the way.

stops.name: ρ Cassiopeiae

getThere.text: From the Garnet Star, slide up about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (17°) to ρ Cassiopeiae, in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: ρ Cassiopeiae, a faint star near Caph, and η Cassiopeiae in the W have surfaces of about the same temperature, which makes the pair a clean test of size once you see past a tint that dust has warmed.
stops.transitionText: The Garnet Star turned color into the heat of each patch of surface, and at ρ Cassiopeiae the star's true power, set beside that heat, gives away how much surface there is.

card.question: How can a star you can barely see be one of the sky’s most powerful?
card.glance: A faint yellowish star near Caph in Cassiopeia that looks entirely ordinary.
card.see: Start at Caph, the western end of Cassiopeia’s W, and slide about two and a half degrees west-south-west to a faint yellowish star. σ Cassiopeiae lies just south, with the soft glow of Caroline’s Rose between them.
card.understand: Most stars that look bright are simply close, and ρ Cas is the opposite case. Astronomers fix its distance from the family of stars it travels with and measure its true width with interferometers, and together those give its real output. A star this extreme, roughly 40 times the Sun’s mass, lives in a brief, unstable late stage, and in 2000 it dimmed, cooled sharply and threw off a shell of gas.
card.answer: From about 9,000 light-years away, a star needs more than half a million times the Sun’s output to reach your eye at all, and ρ Cassiopeiae has it. The faint dot near Caph is one of the most luminous stars you can see.
card.wonder: That single outburst in 2000 shed gas weighing roughly 10,000 Earths.
card.connect: Power, not closeness, puts it in your sky: η Cassiopeiae, brighter to the eye, is only about 19 light-years away.

lens.beat: The Sun's heat, a giant's size
lens.question: ρ and η Cassiopeiae are about equally hot; why is one so much stronger?
lens.why: ρ Cassiopeiae, a faint star near Caph, and η Cassiopeiae in the W have surfaces of about the same temperature, which makes the pair a clean test of size once you see past a tint that dust has warmed.
lens.look: Start at Caph and slide about two and a half degrees west-south-west to ρ Cassiopeiae, a faint yellow-orange point. Then swing back east to η Cassiopeiae, between Schedar and γ in the W, a brighter, paler yellow star. ρ looks the warmer of the two, partly because dust along its long path reddens it.
lens.answer: At one temperature a star's light grows with its surface, and ρ Cassiopeiae gives out about half a million times η's light, so it must be some 560 times η's width, a hypergiant beside a near twin of the Sun. The clues can weigh up that gap, yet not explain how two stars of one heat came to differ so much, and that takes stars of one age and one distance.
lens.story: Dust between the stars scatters blue light more than red, as the air does at sunset, so a star seen through thousands of light-years of it looks warmer in tint than it is. That is why astronomers read ρ Cassiopeiae's temperature from the dark lines in its spectrum rather than from its color, and those lines put its surface close to the Sun's.

stops.name: Double Cluster (h Persei)

getThere.text: Move up and to the right about three fields of your 6.5° binoculars (19°), and the Double Cluster (h Persei) is there, in Perseus.

stops.whyHere: The Double Cluster packs hundreds of stars with one birthday into a single binocular field, so the few that look different are telling you about weight, not age.
stops.transitionText: Size explained the light of ρ Cassiopeiae, and the Double Cluster shows where such differences come from, because in a family of stars born together the heavy ones change first.

card.question: Why do a few orange stars shine among the Double Cluster’s blue-white crowd?
card.glance: Two rich swarms of stars side by side in one view between Cassiopeia and Perseus, a naked-eye smudge from a dark site.
card.see: Sweep from Cassiopeia’s W toward Perseus and two glittering knots appear in one field, each crowded with dozens of points, the western one, h Persei, a little richer in the middle. Look for a few orange stars among the blue-white, especially toward the eastern cluster.
card.understand: Both clusters formed in the same burst of star birth, so all their stars share a birthday. Most are hot blue-white stars many times heavier than the Sun, and the orange points are the heaviest of all. Weight is destiny for a star: the more massive it is, the faster it burns, so those few have already raced to their last chapter.
card.answer: The orange stars were born with the rest, but being the heaviest they aged fastest and have swollen into red supergiants, cool on the surface and orange in color. Their ages, read from the supergiants alone, match the cluster’s, a neat cross-check.
card.wonder: They lie about 7,400 light-years away, more than ten times farther than the Pleiades, yet are still bright enough to see without binoculars.
card.connect: Its twin, χ Persei, sits half a degree east, born of the same cloud at the same time.

lens.beat: Heavy stars live fast
lens.question: In a family only 14 million years old, how can some stars already be giants?
lens.why: The Double Cluster packs hundreds of stars with one birthday into a single binocular field, so the few that look different are telling you about weight, not age.
lens.look: Sweep from Cassiopeia's W toward Perseus and hold both clusters in one field. Among the blue-white crowd pick out a few orange points, mostly around and east of the pair, and defocus a touch so their color shows as small warm disks.
lens.answer: Only the very heaviest stars could use up their core hydrogen so quickly, and these few have already swollen into red supergiants while their lighter siblings still burn blue-white. lens.story: A star's light climbs much more steeply than its weight, so a heavier star spends its larger store of fuel far faster and has the shorter life. Put those two clues together and the orange points come out as the largest stars in the family, bloated giants among compact blue-white ones.

card.question: Why is Mirfak yellower than the blue-white stars that surround it?
card.glance: The brightest star of Perseus, yellow-white and ringed in binoculars by a swarm of blue-white stars.
card.see: Aim at Mirfak, between Capella and Cassiopeia’s W, and the field fills with dozens of blue-white stars strung in curving chains, with Mirfak a shade yellower than the rest. Wide, low-power binoculars frame this cluster better than any telescope.
card.understand: An open cluster is a family of stars born together from one gas cloud, so its members share a birthday and a distance. That makes it a natural experiment in which the one big difference is how much mass each star started with. Heavy stars burn their fuel disproportionately fast, so the heaviest runs out of core hydrogen first and swells while its lighter siblings carry on.
card.answer: Mirfak started out the heaviest of the family, about seven times the Sun’s mass, so it has already swollen into a yellow supergiant while its siblings still shine blue-white, all within some tens of millions of years.
card.wonder: Mirfak and its siblings still travel through space together, a family that has stayed close for tens of millions of years.
card.connect: In the older Pleiades, stars as heavy as Mirfak have already burned out.
